doctrines.name: Modern Movements
doctrines.question: How should Christianity respond to modernity, and who now speaks for it?
doctrines.summary: From Schleiermacher to deconstruction, modern Christianity has been shaped by responses to critical scholarship, science and secularisation (liberalism, fundamentalism, neo-orthodoxy, evangelicalism), by the quest for unity (ecumenism), by new restoration movements (Stone-Campbell; Latter-day Saints and Jehovah’s Witnesses, outside Nicene orthodoxy), and by the shift of Christianity’s centre to the Global South.
doctrines.longText:
The Enlightenment and the rise of historical criticism, Darwinian science and secular states posed a new kind of question: not which doctrine is true, but whether and how traditional Christianity can be believed at all by modern people. Friedrich Schleiermacher grounded faith in religious experience; Ritschl and Harnack sought the kernel of the gospel in Jesus’ ethic of love. Catholic Modernists attempted something similar and were condemned by Pius X in 1907. In America, fundamentalists answered with The Fundamentals (1910–15) and the battle for inerrancy, culminating in the Fundamentalist–Modernist controversy and the Scopes trial (1925).

The First World War shattered liberal optimism. Karl Barth’s Epistle to the Romans (1919/1922) launched neo-orthodoxy, insisting on God’s otherness and the sole lordship of Christ, which became a confession of resistance at Barmen (1934). Meanwhile conservative Protestants regrouped as a non-separatist "new evangelicalism" (NAE 1942; Billy Graham; Lausanne 1974), and the ecumenical movement, born at Edinburgh in 1910, produced the World Council of Churches (1948) and, after Vatican II, a transformed relationship between Catholics, Orthodox and Protestants.

The 19th-century American frontier also produced restoration movements. Barton Stone and the Campbells sought unity by restoring New Testament Christianity within Nicene faith. Joseph Smith’s Latter-day Saints (1830) and Charles Taze Russell’s Bible Students, later Jehovah’s Witnesses (1879/1931), claimed restorations that rejected the Nicene doctrine of God; they are described here in their own terms but labelled, as the historic churches regard them, as outside historic Nicene orthodoxy.

The most important development of the century, however, was geographical. In 1910 two-thirds of Christians lived in Europe; by 2010 about a quarter did. African prophets and Instituted Churches, Latin American Pentecostals, Korean and Indian churches and the Chinese house churches, which survived the Cultural Revolution, made Christianity a predominantly non-Western faith. In the West, by contrast, secularisation, emerging and progressive movements and the "deconstruction" of evangelical faith reshape the landscape. This section maps these movements, their arguments and their critics.

nodes.label: How should Christianity respond to modernity, and who now speaks for it?
nodes.text: Since the Enlightenment, Christians have faced historical criticism of the Bible, Darwinian science, secularisation, world wars, the end of Christendom and the southward shift of the faith. Should doctrine be reinterpreted for modern people, defended unchanged, or rediscovered? Should divided churches seek visible unity? Do new revelations or restorations supersede the historic churches? And where, demographically, is Christianity’s future?

nodes.label: John 17:21: "That they all may be one"
nodes.text: Jesus’ prayer for unity is the charter text of the ecumenical movement.

nodes.label: Acts 2:42–47 and the New Testament pattern
nodes.text: The apostles’ teaching, breaking of bread, prayers and house fellowship: the model Restorationists, house churches and primitivist movements seek to recover.

nodes.label: 2 Timothy 3:16 and Jude 3: inspired Scripture, "the faith once delivered"
nodes.text: Fundamentalists cite these for an inerrant Bible and an unchanging deposit; liberals ask how inspiration relates to historical criticism. (Dates of 2 Timothy and Jude are debated, c.65–90.)

nodes.label: Schleiermacher: religion as the feeling of absolute dependence (1799–1830)
nodes.text: On Religion: Speeches to Its Cultured Despisers (1799) and The Christian Faith (1821–22) ground theology in religious experience rather than metaphysics or an infallible text: the father of liberal Protestantism.

nodes.label: Thomas Campbell: "Where the Scriptures speak, we speak" (1809)
nodes.text: On the American frontier, Restorationists seek unity by discarding creeds and restoring New Testament Christianity.

nodes.label: Restorationism (Stone-Campbell)
nodes.text: Barton Stone’s "Christians" and the Campbells’ "Disciples" unite in 1832.

nodes.label: Latter-day Saint restoration (outside Nicene orthodoxy)
nodes.text: Joseph Smith publishes the Book of Mormon and organises the Church of Christ (later The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints) in 1830, claiming a restoration after a Great Apostasy.

nodes.label: Jehovah’s Witnesses (outside Nicene orthodoxy)
nodes.text: From the Adventist milieu after 1844, Charles Taze Russell’s Bible Students begin publishing Zion’s Watch Tower (1879); renamed Jehovah’s Witnesses in 1931.

nodes.label: Liberal Protestantism (and Catholic Modernism)
nodes.text: Ritschl and Harnack: the kernel of the gospel is the fatherhood of God, the value of the soul and love; dogma and miracle are its historical husk.

nodes.label: Rome condemns Modernism (1907)
nodes.text: Lamentabili and Pascendi condemn Loisy, Tyrrell and others; the Anti-Modernist Oath binds Catholic clergy from 1910 until 1967.

nodes.label: World Missionary Conference, Edinburgh (1910)
nodes.text: Some 1,200 delegates (only about 18 from Asia, and none from Africa) plan cooperation in world mission; its continuation committee leads to the International Missionary Council and the WCC.

nodes.label: The Fundamentals and the "five fundamentals" (1910)
nodes.text: The Presbyterian General Assembly affirms inerrancy, the virgin birth, substitutionary atonement, the bodily resurrection and the reality of miracles; the essay series The Fundamentals (1910–15) is sent free to pastors worldwide.

nodes.label: Fundamentalism
nodes.text: Coined in 1920 by the Baptist editor Curtis Lee Laws for those ready "to do battle royal for the fundamentals".

nodes.label: Fosdick vs Machen: tolerance or two religions? (1922–23)
nodes.text: Fosdick pleads for liberty for modern believers; Machen replies that liberalism is not Christianity at all. The Auburn Affirmation (1924), signed by about 1,300 Presbyterian ministers, defends theological liberty.

nodes.label: Scopes trial and fundamentalist retreat (1925)
nodes.text: The prosecution of a Tennessee teacher for teaching evolution makes fundamentalism a national spectacle; fundamentalists lose control of northern denominations (Princeton reorganised 1929) and build separate institutions.

nodes.label: Neo-orthodoxy (dialectical theology)
nodes.text: Karl Barth’s Romans (1919/1922) breaks with liberalism after its leaders back the war of 1914: God’s Word judges all human religion.

nodes.label: Barmen Declaration (1934)
nodes.text: Neo-orthodox theology becomes a confession of resistance against the Nazi "German Christians".

nodes.label: Evangelicalism (neo-evangelical)
nodes.text: The National Association of Evangelicals (1942), Fuller Seminary (1947), Billy Graham’s crusades (from 1949) and Christianity Today (1956) present an engaged, non-separatist conservative Protestantism.

nodes.label: World Council of Churches founded (1948)
nodes.text: 147 churches meet at Amsterdam: Protestant, Anglican, Old Catholic and several Orthodox churches; the Church of South India (1947) shows organic union of Anglicans, Methodists and Reformed.

nodes.label: The ecumenical movement
nodes.text: Visible unity in faith, sacraments and mission as the goal of divided churches.

nodes.label: Second Vatican Council enters the ecumenical movement (1962–65)
nodes.text: Unitatis Redintegratio (1964); mutual lifting of the 1054 anathemas by Paul VI and Athenagoras (1965); later the Joint Declaration on Justification (1999).

nodes.label: Lausanne Congress on World Evangelization (1974)
nodes.text: 2,700 participants from 150 countries; Latin Americans René Padilla and Samuel Escobar push evangelicals towards "integral mission".

nodes.label: Persecution and the Chinese house churches (1966–76)
nodes.text: All public worship is closed during the Cultural Revolution; Christianity survives and grows in homes, emerging after 1979 as a vast unregistered movement alongside the state-sanctioned Three-Self churches.

nodes.label: House-church movements
nodes.text: Small, lay-led, often unregistered congregations meeting in homes: China, Iran, and Western "simple church" networks.

nodes.label: Global South Christianity
nodes.text: By about 1980 more Christians live in Africa, Asia and Latin America than in Europe and North America; African Instituted, Pentecostal and indigenous churches reshape the faith.

nodes.label: Emerging and progressive Christianity
nodes.text: Brian McLaren’s A New Kind of Christian (2001), Emergent Village, the UK’s Fresh Expressions (2004) and later progressive Christianity.

nodes.label: Deconstruction
nodes.text: Mostly Western, mostly ex-evangelical re-examination of inherited faith, amplified by social media (#exvangelical, 2016), abuse scandals and politics.

nodes.label: Where Christians live (2010s–2020s)
nodes.text: In 1910 about two-thirds of the world’s Christians lived in Europe; by 2010 about a quarter did, with roughly 24% in Latin America, 24% in sub-Saharan Africa and 13% in Asia-Pacific (Pew 2011). Africa now has the largest Christian population of any continent (World Christian Database).

nodes.label: Today: realignment rather than resolution
nodes.text: Liberal and conservative Protestants increasingly align across denominations (e.g. GAFCON 2008; Global Methodist Church 2022); ecumenical dialogue continues alongside evangelical–Catholic cooperation on moral issues; the Latter-day Saints (about 17 million members, 2023) and Jehovah’s Witnesses (about 8.8 million publishers, 2024) remain outside the Nicene churches’ fellowship; in the US the Christian share fell to about 62% but appeared to stabilise (Pew Religious Landscape Study, 2025).

positions.name: Liberal Protestantism (and Catholic Modernism)
positions.oneLine: Christian faith must be reinterpreted in the light of modern knowledge (historical criticism, science, philosophy), locating its essence in religious experience and the ethical teaching of Jesus rather than in dogma or an infallible text.
coreClaims: Religion is grounded in experience (Schleiermacher’s feeling of absolute dependence) or moral value (Ritschl), not in authoritative propositions.
The Bible is a human record of revelation, to be studied with the same historical-critical methods as other texts.
Doctrines are historically conditioned expressions of faith that can and should be restated.
The heart of the gospel is the fatherhood of God, the infinite value of the human soul and the ethic of love (Harnack).
God works immanently through history, evolution and human progress.
positions.origin: Rooted in the Enlightenment and Romanticism, it was founded as a theological movement by Friedrich Schleiermacher (On Religion, 1799; The Christian Faith, 1821–22), developed by Albrecht Ritschl and Adolf von Harnack in Germany, Horace Bushnell and the Social Gospel in America, and by Catholic Modernists (Alfred Loisy, George Tyrrell) until condemned by Pius X (1907). 20th-century heirs include Rudolf Bultmann’s demythologising (1941), Paul Tillich and process and progressive theologies.
strongestArguments: It takes honest intellectual inquiry seriously and refuses to set faith against established historical and scientific knowledge.
It makes Christianity intelligible and credible to educated modern people, as earlier theologians did for Platonists and Aristotelians.
It recovers the ethical, this-worldly emphasis of Jesus and the prophets, fuelling social reform.
It recognises the human, historical character of Scripture and doctrine, which the Bible itself displays.
strongestObjections: Machen and other critics argue it is "a totally diverse type of religious belief" that keeps Christian words while abandoning the redemptive supernatural faith.
Karl Barth argued that grounding theology in human experience made God a projection of human culture, as shown by liberal theologians’ support for the German war in 1914.

Its optimism about progress was shattered by the World Wars; H. Richard Niebuhr caricatured it as preaching "a God without wrath" bringing "men without sin into a kingdom without judgment through the ministrations of a Christ without a cross."
Sociologically, liberal denominations have declined steeply in membership since the 1960s.
responses: Liberals reply that the "essence" of Christianity has always been reinterpreted and that rigid orthodoxy, not liberalism, drives modern people away.
Post-liberal and progressive heirs have accepted many criticisms of naive progressivism while maintaining critical engagement with Scripture and science.
Membership decline reflects many factors (birth rates, secularisation) rather than theology alone.
consequences: Dominated leading Protestant universities and seminaries in Europe and North America by 1900.
Provoked the fundamentalist reaction and Catholic anti-Modernism, and later Barth’s neo-orthodoxy.
Shaped mainline Protestant churches, the Social Gospel and the ecumenical movement.
Historical-critical methods it championed became standard in academic biblical studies across traditions.

positions.name: Fundamentalism
positions.oneLine: Christians must defend the non-negotiable "fundamentals" of historic faith (an inerrant Bible, the virgin birth, substitutionary atonement, bodily resurrection, miracles and Christ’s return) against modernism, and separate from churches that deny them.
coreClaims: The Bible is verbally inspired and inerrant in its original manuscripts.
The virgin birth, substitutionary atonement, bodily resurrection, miracles and the personal return of Christ are essential.
Modernist theology is apostasy, not an acceptable variant of Christianity.
Faithful Christians must contend for the faith and, where necessary, separate from apostate institutions (ecclesiastical separation).
Usually premillennial, often dispensational, with strong emphasis on evangelism.
positions.origin: Emerged from 19th-century premillennial Bible conferences (Niagara, 1878), Princeton inerrancy (A. A. Hodge and B. B. Warfield, 1881) and opposition to higher criticism. The Presbyterian General Assembly’s five fundamentals (1910) and The Fundamentals (1910–15) gave it a platform; Curtis Lee Laws coined the name in 1920; William Bell Riley’s World’s Christian Fundamentals Association (1919), the Scopes trial (1925) and the founding of separatist bodies (Orthodox Presbyterian Church, 1936; Bob Jones University) followed. The term is now also applied, often loosely, to conservative movements in other religions.
strongestArguments: It defended doctrines held by virtually all Christians for nineteen centuries and confessed in the creeds against those who denied them.
Its leaders included serious scholars (Machen, Warfield) whose arguments that liberalism was a different religion were acknowledged even by some secular observers.
It sustained vigorous missions, Bible institutes and evangelism when mainline zeal was declining.
It saw early that institutional drift could empty churches of their founding faith.
strongestObjections: Critics argue that it made secondary matters (a particular inerrancy theory, premillennialism, young-earth creationism) into tests of faith.
Separatism produced endless splits, harsh polemics and anti-intellectualism, as later evangelicals such as Carl Henry (The Uneasy Conscience of Modern Fundamentalism, 1947) lamented.
Its "defence" of Scripture sometimes relied on modern rationalist assumptions (Baconian common-sense realism) rather than historic doctrine.
Its political turn (Moral Majority) is criticised for fusing faith with partisan politics.
responses: Fundamentalists reply that the essentials they defended were not novel but confessional, and that separation from denial of the gospel is commanded (2 Cor 6:17; 2 John 10).
Many acknowledge excesses of militancy while insisting that the core doctrinal concerns were vindicated by the decline of liberal churches.
consequences: Lost control of the northern Presbyterian and Baptist denominations in the 1920s–30s, then built a parallel network of schools, radio and missions.
Gave rise, via reform from within, to the neo-evangelical movement of the 1940s.
Shaped American creationism debates and the Religious Right.
Exported to mission fields, influencing churches in Africa, Asia and Latin America.

positions.name: Neo-orthodoxy (dialectical theology)
altNames: Theology of the Word of God
positions.oneLine: Against liberalism, God is "wholly other" and known only through his self-revelation in Jesus Christ, the one Word of God attested by Scripture and proclaimed by the Church, which judges all human religion and culture.
coreClaims: God is known only by God’s free self-revelation, not by natural theology or religious experience.
Jesus Christ is the one Word of God; Scripture is the witness to that Word and becomes God’s Word as God speaks through it.
Human sin and the crisis of judgement are taken with radical seriousness; grace is God’s free act.
The Church exists to hear and proclaim the Word, independent of state and culture.
In Barth’s mature theology, election is God’s choice of all humanity in Christ.
positions.origin: Triggered by the support of Karl Barth’s liberal teachers for the German war effort (manifesto of 93 intellectuals, 1914). Barth’s Epistle to the Romans (1919; rewritten 1922), with Eduard Thurneysen, Friedrich Gogarten and Emil Brunner, launched "dialectical theology"; Barth’s Church Dogmatics (1932–67) developed it. In the US, Reinhold and H. Richard Niebuhr represented a related "Christian realism". Its political expression was the Barmen Declaration (1934).
strongestArguments: It recovered the transcendence and freedom of God and the centrality of Christ after liberalism’s collapse in 1914.
Its stress on the Word over culture enabled the Confessing Church’s resistance to Nazism.
It reconnected modern theology with the Reformers and the Fathers while accepting historical criticism.
Barth’s Church Dogmatics is widely regarded as the most important Protestant theology of the 20th century.
strongestObjections: Conservative evangelicals (Cornelius Van Til, The New Modernism, 1946; Carl Henry) objected that saying Scripture "becomes" the Word of God undermines its objective inspiration and inerrancy.
Liberals and existentialists (Bultmann, Tillich) found it fideist, cutting faith off from reason and culture; Brunner disputed its rejection of natural theology (Barth’s "Nein!", 1934).
Catholic and evangelical critics worry that Barth’s doctrine of election tends toward universalism.
responses: Barthians reply that Scripture’s authority rests on God’s living speech through it, not on a theory of inerrancy, and that this is closer to the Reformers.
Barth insisted he did not teach universalism as a doctrine, leaving final outcomes to God’s freedom while hoping for all.
consequences: Shaped mid-20th-century mainline Protestant theology, ecumenism (WCC) and seminaries worldwide.
Grounded the Barmen Declaration and later confessions of resistance (e.g. Belhar, 1986).
Barth’s influence revived from the 1990s among evangelicals and in Trinitarian theology (T. F. Torrance).

positions.name: Evangelicalism
positions.oneLine: A transdenominational Protestant movement marked by conversion, the authority of the Bible, the centrality of Christ’s cross and active evangelism and service, seeking to engage the world rather than withdraw from it.
coreClaims: Conversionism: lives need to be changed by personal faith in Christ.
Biblicism: the Bible is the supreme authority for faith and life.
Crucicentrism: Christ’s atoning death is the heart of the gospel.
Activism: the gospel must be expressed in evangelism, mission and service (Bebbington’s quadrilateral).
Cooperation across denominations on the basis of shared essentials.
positions.origin: Rooted in the 18th-century revivals (Edwards, Whitefield, Wesley) and 19th-century missionary and reform movements. After the fundamentalist–modernist split, "new evangelicals" (Harold Ockenga, Carl F. H. Henry, Billy Graham) formed the National Association of Evangelicals (1942), Fuller Theological Seminary (1947) and Christianity Today (1956). The Lausanne Congress (1974) globalised it, with Latin American, African and Asian voices shaping "integral mission".
strongestArguments: It combines historic Protestant orthodoxy with energetic mission, producing one of the fastest-growing Christian movements worldwide.
Its transdenominational character allows cooperation in evangelism, relief and Bible translation.
Through Lausanne it integrated evangelism and social responsibility.
It engages scholarship and culture rather than retreating into separatism.
strongestObjections: Fundamentalists criticise its cooperation with liberals and Catholics (e.g. Graham’s 1957 New York crusade).
Catholic, Orthodox and mainline critics argue it is individualistic, weak on ecclesiology and sacraments, and prone to consumerism and celebrity culture.
In the US its close association with partisan politics since the 1980s has, critics argue, compromised its witness; scandals of abuse and authoritarian leadership have damaged trust.
Scholars dispute whether "evangelical" names a coherent theological movement or a political-cultural identity.
responses: Evangelicals reply that cooperation in proclamation does not imply doctrinal compromise and that the gospel transcends denominations.
Global evangelical leaders stress that most evangelicals now live in the Global South, where the political profile is different from the US.
consequences: Became one of the largest Christian movements: Pew (2011) estimated about 285 million evangelicals (about 13% of Christians) in 2010, with broader definitions giving higher figures.
Shaped global missions, Bible translation, relief agencies (World Vision, Tearfund) and media.
Became a major political force in the US, Brazil and elsewhere.

positions.name: The ecumenical movement
positions.oneLine: Divided churches should seek visible unity in faith, sacraments, ministry and mission, as Christ prayed "that they all may be one".
coreClaims: Christian division contradicts Christ’s will and hinders mission (John 17:21).
Churches should pray, study, work and witness together and pursue doctrinal agreement through dialogue.
Mutual recognition of baptism is the basis of a real though imperfect communion.
The goal (variously understood) is visible unity: organic union, reconciled diversity or full communion.
positions.origin: Grew from 19th-century missionary cooperation, student movements and the Evangelical Alliance (1846). The World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh (1910) led to the Life and Work (Stockholm 1925) and Faith and Order (Lausanne 1927) movements, which merged in the World Council of Churches (Amsterdam, 1948). Church unions followed (United Church of Canada 1925; Church of South India 1947; Church of North India 1970). The Catholic Church entered with Vatican II’s Unitatis Redintegratio (1964); key fruits include the lifting of the 1054 anathemas (1965), BEM (1982) and the Joint Declaration on Justification (1999).
strongestArguments: Jesus prayed for his disciples’ unity "that the world may believe"; division is a scandal to mission.
Dialogue has resolved or softened historic disputes (e.g. justification 1999; Christological agreements with the Oriental Orthodox and the Assyrian Church of the East, 1994).
Shared witness has strengthened Christians’ response to persecution, injustice (apartheid) and poverty.
strongestObjections: Conservative evangelicals and fundamentalists argue that it subordinates truth to unity and includes churches that deny essential doctrines.
Some Orthodox (Georgia and Bulgaria left the WCC in 1997–98) and traditionalist Catholics see it as relativising the one true Church.
Critics charge the WCC with political partisanship (e.g. Programme to Combat Racism grants to liberation movements, 1970s).
Institutional ecumenism has stalled on ministry and Eucharist, and new divisions over sexuality have arisen.
responses: Ecumenists reply that unity is sought "in truth" through rigorous theological dialogue, not minimalism.
They point to grassroots and "receptive" ecumenism and to forums such as the Global Christian Forum (2007), which include Pentecostals and evangelicals.
consequences: Produced the WCC, national councils and many bilateral dialogues.
Transformed Catholic–Protestant and Catholic–Orthodox relations from hostility to fraternity.
Created united churches, notably in South Asia.
Provoked separate evangelical and fundamentalist networks (e.g. International Council of Christian Churches, 1948).

positions.name: Restorationism
positions.oneLine: The Church should restore the faith and practice of the New Testament church, setting aside later creeds, denominations and traditions, so that Christians can unite on the Bible alone.
coreClaims: The New Testament provides a pattern for church doctrine, worship and organisation.
Human creeds should not be tests of fellowship; "no creed but Christ, no book but the Bible".
Believers’ baptism by immersion "for the remission of sins" (Acts 2:38).
Weekly celebration of the Lord’s Supper.
Congregational autonomy with elders and deacons; use of Bible names for Bible things ("Christians", "churches of Christ").
positions.origin: A broad primitivist impulse runs through Christian history (Waldensians, Anabaptists, Brethren), but the American Restoration Movement began with Barton W. Stone (after the Cane Ridge revival, 1801; the Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery, 1804) and Thomas and Alexander Campbell (Declaration and Address, 1809); their movements united in Lexington, Kentucky, in 1832. It divided into the Churches of Christ (a cappella, formally recognised 1906), the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ) and the independent Christian churches/churches of Christ. Many later movements (Adventists, Latter-day Saints, Pentecostals with their "apostolic faith") share restorationist premises.
strongestArguments: Scripture is the only universally accepted Christian authority, so it is the natural basis for unity.
Many historic divisions arise from post-biblical creeds and traditions.
It honours the Reformation principle of sola scriptura consistently.
Its emphasis on weekly communion and immersion reflects strong early-church evidence.
strongestObjections: Historic churches argue that "no creed but the Bible" is itself a creed, and that the Bible must be interpreted within the community and its rule of faith, as the creeds do.
Ironically the movement itself split repeatedly (over instruments, missionary societies, theology).
Critics argue its teaching on baptism for remission of sins approaches baptismal regeneration and can foster legalism.
The New Testament may not provide a single, detailed blueprint for church order.
responses: Restorationists reply that their aim is not to deny historic Christianity but to subordinate all traditions to Scripture.
Many now combine restorationist ideals with ecumenical engagement (the Disciples were founding members of the WCC).
consequences: Produced one of the largest American-born Christian movements, with millions of members in the US and growing churches in Africa, India and the Philippines.
Its primitivist logic, taken further, contributed to new religious movements claiming a fuller restoration.
The Disciples became a mainline ecumenical denomination; Churches of Christ remained conservative.

positions.name: Latter-day Saint restoration (outside historic Nicene orthodoxy)
altNames: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
Mormonism (a name the church now asks to avoid)
positions.oneLine: Latter-day Saints believe that after a "Great Apostasy" God restored the original Church of Jesus Christ through the prophet Joseph Smith, with renewed priesthood authority, additional scripture and continuing revelation. Its teaching on God departs from the Nicene Creed, and Nicene churches do not regard it as within historic orthodoxy.
coreClaims: The early Church fell into apostasy, losing priesthood authority; God restored it through Joseph Smith (first vision 1820; church organised 6 April 1830).
The Book of Mormon, Doctrine and Covenants and Pearl of Great Price are scripture alongside the Bible "as far as it is translated correctly".
The Godhead consists of three distinct divine beings united in purpose; the Father has a glorified body of flesh and bone (Doctrine and Covenants 130:22).
Humans existed premortally as spirit children of heavenly parents and can progress toward exaltation.
Saving ordinances (baptism, temple endowment, sealing) are performed by restored priesthood, including vicariously for the dead.
Living prophets and apostles continue to receive revelation.
keyTexts: Ezekiel 37:15–20 (read as Bible and Book of Mormon)
Book of Mormon; Doctrine and Covenants; Pearl of Great Price
positions.origin: Joseph Smith (1805–1844) emerged from the "burned-over district" of western New York amid revivals and restorationist ferment. He published the Book of Mormon in 1830 and led the church to Ohio, Missouri and Nauvoo, Illinois, where he was killed in 1844. Brigham Young led the majority to Utah (1847); others formed the Reorganized Church (now Community of Christ, 1860). Plural marriage, publicly taught from 1852, was officially ended in 1890; the priesthood restriction on men of Black African descent was lifted in 1978.
strongestArguments: Latter-day Saints argue that the proliferation of Christian denominations shows the need for restored divine authority and revelation (Joseph Smith’s question in James 1:5).
They point to the New Testament pattern of apostles, prophets and continuing revelation, which they believe historic churches lost.
They cite the lived fruit of the church: family life, service, missionary dedication and rapid growth to over 17 million members (2023).
strongestObjections: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches hold that its doctrine of God (multiple divine beings, an embodied Father, human exaltation) contradicts biblical monotheism and the Nicene Creed; the Catholic Church ruled LDS baptism invalid in 2001.
Historic Christians reject the claim of a total apostasy, citing Christ’s promise that the gates of hell would not prevail against the Church (Matt 16:18).

Historians and archaeologists find no independent evidence for the Book of Mormon’s ancient American civilisations, and critics raise questions about the Book of Abraham and early church history (polygamy, the 1857 Mountain Meadows massacre).
responses: Latter-day Saints reply that they worship the Father, Son and Holy Ghost and accept Jesus Christ as divine Saviour, and that the Nicene formulations reflect later Greek philosophy.

The church has published essays (Gospel Topics, 2013–15) addressing historical controversies, and LDS scholars defend the Book of Mormon’s antiquity while affirming that its truth is known by spiritual witness (Moroni 10:4).
consequences: Became the largest and most successful religious movement born in the United States, with a majority of members now outside the US.
Shaped the settlement and culture of Utah and the American West.
Its relationship to historic Christianity remains disputed: it calls itself Christian, while Nicene churches classify it as a distinct restorationist religion outside historic orthodoxy.

positions.name: Jehovah’s Witnesses (outside historic Nicene orthodoxy)
positions.oneLine: Jehovah’s Witnesses believe they have restored true Bible teaching: Jehovah alone is Almighty God, Jesus is his first created Son, Christ’s invisible kingdom rule began in 1914, and Armageddon will soon usher in an earthly paradise. Their rejection of the Trinity places them outside historic Nicene orthodoxy.
coreClaims: Jehovah is the only true God; the Trinity is an unbiblical, post-apostolic doctrine.
Jesus is God’s firstborn creation, identified with Michael the archangel, who died on a stake as a ransom.
The holy spirit is God’s active force, not a person.
Christ began ruling invisibly in heaven in 1914; the present system will end soon at Armageddon.
144,000 anointed Christians will rule in heaven; a "great crowd" will live forever on a paradise earth; the wicked are annihilated, not tormented.
Members avoid blood transfusions, military service and political involvement, and witness door to door.
positions.origin: Charles Taze Russell (1852–1916), influenced by Adventist preachers in the post-1844 Millerite milieu, founded a Bible study group in Pittsburgh (c.1870) and Zion’s Watch Tower (1879). Under Joseph F. Rutherford the movement centralised and took the name Jehovah’s Witnesses (1931). The New World Translation appeared in 1950–61. Witnesses were persecuted in Nazi Germany (marked with a purple triangle in camps), and have been banned in the Soviet Union and in Russia since 2017.
strongestArguments: Witnesses argue that strict monotheism is the plain teaching of both Testaments and that Trinitarian formulas are absent from Scripture.
They cite texts where Jesus calls the Father "greater" (John 14:28) or is called "firstborn of all creation" (Col 1:15).
Their commitment to neutrality and nonviolence (e.g. refusing to fight in Nazi Germany) and their evangelistic zeal are widely admired.
strongestObjections: Nicene churches regard their Christology as a form of Arianism condemned at Nicaea (325), and cite texts calling Christ God (John 1:1; 20:28; Titus 2:13; Heb 1:8).
Scholars criticise the New World Translation’s renderings (e.g. "a god" in John 1:1) as theologically driven.
Failed or revised expectations (1914, 1925, 1975) and the redefinition of "this generation" are cited by critics and ex-members.

Practices such as shunning disfellowshipped members and refusing blood transfusions have drawn criticism, and child-abuse handling has been examined by courts and inquiries (e.g. Australian Royal Commission, 2015).
responses: Witnesses reply that their translation follows the Greek grammar faithfully and restores the divine name.
They maintain that adjusting understanding as "the light gets brighter" (Prov 4:18) is part of faithful Bible study, not failed prophecy.
consequences: Grew to about 8.8 million active publishers in some 240 lands (2024 service year).
Their legal battles produced landmark religious-liberty rulings (e.g. US Supreme Court, West Virginia v. Barnette, 1943).
Remain separate from all other churches, which in turn classify them outside historic Christian orthodoxy.

positions.name: Global South Christianity
positions.oneLine: Christianity’s demographic and increasingly theological centre has moved to Africa, Latin America and Asia, where churches are typically Spirit-oriented, biblically and morally conservative, holistic and self-theologising.
coreClaims: Christianity is a translatable faith that becomes at home in every culture (Walls, Sanneh).
Most Christians now live in the Global South, and their experience should shape theology, not only Western debates.
Many Southern churches emphasise the Holy Spirit, healing, deliverance and the reality of the spirit world.
Theology must address poverty, power, ancestors, other religions and nation-building in context.
Southern churches increasingly send missionaries to the West ("reverse mission").
positions.origin: The roots are ancient (Ethiopia, Egypt, India, the Church of the East), but the modern shift came through 19th- and 20th-century missions and especially indigenous movements: African prophets (William Wade Harris, 1913; Simon Kimbangu, 1921), African Instituted Churches, the Korean revivals (1907), Chinese indigenous churches (Watchman Nee, John Sung) and Latin American Pentecostalism (Chile, 1909; Brazil, 1911). After decolonisation, Christianity in Africa grew from about 10 million (1900) to several hundred million. Pew (2011) found that the share of Christians in Europe fell from about two-thirds in 1910 to about a quarter in 2010.
strongestArguments: Demography: Africa now has more Christians than any other continent, and Latin America and Asia hold hundreds of millions more.
Indigenous leadership and vernacular Scripture have made Christianity an African, Asian and Latin American religion, not a Western import.
Southern churches often embody New Testament vitality: growth, evangelism, healing, community under persecution.
strongestObjections: Critics warn of prosperity theology, authoritarian "big man" leadership and syncretism in some fast-growing churches.
Western progressive critics object to Southern churches’ conservative sexual ethics (e.g. in the Anglican Communion conflict).
Some scholars caution against generalising about a vast, diverse "Global South" or ignoring its long Orthodox and Catholic histories.
responses: Southern theologians reply that discernment of syncretism applies equally to Western accommodation to secular culture.
They insist that Southern Christians must be heard as theologians in their own right, not merely as objects of Western concern.
consequences: Reshaped world Christian demography, mission and leadership (e.g. the first Latin American pope, 2013).
Realigned Anglican and Methodist communions (GAFCON 2008; Global Methodist Church 2022).
Brought new questions (ancestors, polygamy, spiritual warfare, poverty) to the centre of theology.

positions.name: House-church movements
positions.oneLine: Christians can and often should gather as small, lay-led congregations in homes, as in the New Testament, especially under persecution or as an alternative to institutional churches.
coreClaims: The New Testament church met in houses (Rom 16:5; Philemon 2); the home is a legitimate full church.
Every member participates; leadership is plural and largely lay.
Under hostile governments, unregistered house churches preserve faith and obedience to Christ over the state.
Small groups multiply rapidly and foster discipleship.
positions.origin: In China, after the founding of the state-supervised Three-Self Patriotic Movement (1954), leaders such as Wang Mingdao and Watchman Nee refused to join and were imprisoned; during the Cultural Revolution (1966–76) all public worship ceased and faith survived in homes, growing rapidly after 1979 into large networks (e.g. in Henan and Wenzhou). Iranian house churches grew after 1979. In the West, the British "house church movement" of the 1970s (later New Churches) and later "simple" or "organic" church networks (Wolfgang Simson, Frank Viola) drew on the same model.
proponentsOther: Wang Yi (Early Rain Covenant Church, sentenced 2019)
strongestArguments: It follows the New Testament pattern and has proved extraordinarily resilient and fruitful under persecution.
It enables participation of all believers and costs little, suiting poor and persecuted contexts.
It protects the Church’s freedom from state control.
strongestObjections: Critics argue that lack of trained leadership and accountability can foster heresy or cult-like groups (e.g. Eastern Lightning in China, which mainstream house churches reject).
Registered (Three-Self) Christians and some observers argue that registration allows legal stability and open witness.
In the West, critics see "organic church" polemic against institutions as ignoring the historic Church’s wisdom.
responses: House-church networks have developed training, confessions (e.g. the 1998 Confession of Faith of Chinese house-church leaders) and inter-network accountability.
They argue that state registration often involves unacceptable compromises on teaching and evangelism of minors.
consequences: Made China home to one of the world’s largest Christian populations (Pew 2011 estimated about 67 million Christians in China; estimates vary widely).
Provoked recurrent crackdowns (e.g. 2018 regulations, closures of Shouwang and Early Rain churches).
Inspired church-planting strategies globally.

positions.name: Emerging and progressive Christianity
positions.oneLine: Christianity must be re-expressed for a postmodern, pluralist culture: less certainty and boundary-keeping, more conversation, community, justice and inclusion, sometimes with revision of traditional doctrines.
coreClaims: Faith is a journey and conversation, not a closed system of propositions; doubt is welcome.
Following Jesus means embodying the kingdom of God in justice, peace and care for creation.
Church should be missional, contextual and participatory (house churches, pubs, ancient-future liturgy).
Progressive forms revise traditional teaching on hell, atonement, Scripture’s inerrancy and sexuality (full LGBTQ inclusion).
positions.origin: The emerging church arose among younger evangelicals in the US, UK and Australia around 1995–2005: Brian McLaren (A New Kind of Christian, 2001), Emergent Village, Tony Jones, Doug Pagitt, the UK’s alternative worship and Fresh Expressions (Anglican–Methodist, 2004). Progressive Christianity draws also on older liberal traditions (Marcus Borg, John Shelby Spong) and popular authors such as Rob Bell (Love Wins, 2011) and Nadia Bolz-Weber.
strongestArguments: It speaks to people alienated by rigid, politicised or consumerist church cultures.
It recovers neglected emphases: the kingdom, justice, creation care, contemplative practice and ancient liturgy.
It models humility in a pluralist world.
strongestObjections: Evangelical critics (D. A. Carson, Becoming Conversant with the Emerging Church, 2005; DeYoung and Kluck, Why We’re Not Emergent, 2008) argue it undermines truth claims and the authority of Scripture.
Critics note that progressive revisions often reproduce older liberalism, which historically led to decline.
Catholic and Orthodox critics regard it as another fragmentation of Protestant individualism.
responses: Advocates reply that they seek a "generous orthodoxy" and that questioning is a form of faithfulness.
Fresh Expressions shows that missional innovation can occur within traditional churches without doctrinal revision.
consequences: The emerging brand largely dissolved by the mid-2010s, but its practices (missional communities, ancient-future worship) spread widely.
Progressive Christianity became a visible pole in denominational splits over sexuality.
Fed into the deconstruction conversation.

positions.name: Deconstruction (faith deconstruction)
positions.oneLine: A widespread, largely Western and post-evangelical process of critically re-examining inherited beliefs and church culture, which may end in reconstructed faith, a different tradition or leaving Christianity.
coreClaims: Inherited beliefs and practices should be examined honestly rather than accepted on authority.
Harm done by church cultures (abuse, authoritarianism, purity culture, racism, political partisanship) must be named.
Faith can survive and be renewed by questioning ("deconstruct to reconstruct"), though some conclude otherwise.
Personal experience and testimony are important sources of insight.
keyTexts: Jeremiah 1:10 ("to pull down ... to build, and to plant")
positions.origin: The term (borrowed loosely from Jacques Derrida) became popular around 2016–2021 through social media (the #exvangelical hashtag, 2016), podcasts and memoirs (Rachel Held Evans; Josh Harris’ public renunciation in 2019). Drivers include church abuse scandals (e.g. the Mars Hill podcast, 2021; the Southern Baptist Guidepost report, 2022), the politicisation of American evangelicalism, sexuality debates and purity culture. Data show US Christian affiliation falling from about 78% (2007) to about 62% (2023–24), though the decline appeared to level off (Pew 2025).
strongestArguments: Honest examination of belief is biblical ("prove all things") and can lead to a more mature, authentic faith.
It exposes real abuses and hypocrisies that institutions had concealed.
It mirrors historic patterns of reform, protest and doubt within Christianity (the Psalms of lament, the Reformation).
strongestObjections: Critics (e.g. Alisa Childers, Another Gospel?, 2020) argue it often begins from cultural assumptions rather than Scripture and tends toward progressive revisionism or apostasy.
Some argue it is a Western, affluent phenomenon little relevant to most Christians in the Global South.
Pastors worry that online "deconstruction" culture offers critique without community or a path to rebuilding.
responses: Proponents reply that most deconstruction is driven by harm, not fashion, and that churches should listen rather than dismiss.
Many report "reconstruction" in liturgical, Orthodox, Catholic or mainline traditions, or renewed evangelical faith, rather than unbelief.
consequences: Contributed to the growth of the religiously unaffiliated ("nones") in the West.
Led many evangelicals into liturgical, Anglican, Orthodox and Catholic churches.
Prompted churches to address abuse, authoritarian leadership and political entanglement.

controversies.question: Can Christianity be reinterpreted for modern knowledge without ceasing to be Christianity?
controversies.title: The Fundamentalist–Modernist controversy
controversies.summary: In the early 20th century, especially in American Presbyterian and Baptist churches, liberals (modernists) sought to reconcile faith with historical criticism and evolution, while fundamentalists insisted on non-negotiable supernatural doctrines. The conflict reshaped Protestantism into mainline and evangelical camps.

sides.name: Modernists / liberals
sides.steelman: Faith must not require intelligent people to reject what they know about history and science. The abiding experiences of Christianity (trust in God, the way of Jesus, love) can be expressed in changing categories. The church should have room for those who cannot hold a literal virgin birth or inerrant Bible but who love Christ.
arguments: Tolerance and liberty within the church

sides.name: Fundamentalists / conservatives
sides.steelman: Christianity is a historical, redemptive religion: if Christ was not born of a virgin, did not die for our sins and rise bodily, there is no gospel. Liberalism uses Christian words for a different religion. Honesty requires that those who reject the church’s confessions not occupy its pulpits.

sides.name: Neo-orthodox (a third way)
sides.steelman: Both sides grounded faith in something human: liberals in experience, fundamentalists in a theory of the text. The Word of God is Jesus Christ himself, who speaks through Scripture in sovereign freedom and judges both our modern culture and our religious certainties.

timeline.text: A. A. Hodge and B. B. Warfield publish "Inspiration", defining inerrancy of the original autographs.
Charles A. Briggs suspended from the Presbyterian ministry over higher criticism.
Pius X condemns Catholic Modernism.
Presbyterian "five fundamentals"; The Fundamentals begin publication.
Fosdick preaches "Shall the Fundamentalists Win?"
Machen’s Christianity and Liberalism.
Auburn Affirmation defends theological liberty in the Presbyterian Church.
Scopes trial in Dayton, Tennessee.
Princeton Seminary reorganised; Machen founds Westminster Seminary.
Orthodox Presbyterian Church formed.
National Association of Evangelicals founded.
Conservative resurgence begins in the Southern Baptist Convention.

resolution.text: Modernists retained control of the northern mainline denominations; fundamentalists withdrew into separate churches and institutions, from which neo-evangelicalism later emerged. The result was the enduring mainline/evangelical divide in American Protestantism.

consequences: Created the two-party structure of American Protestantism.
Shaped American debates on evolution and education.
Fed later denominational splits and the Religious Right.

controversies.question: Did the historic Church fall into apostasy, requiring a restoration?
controversies.title: Restoration claims and the historic churches
controversies.summary: Many 19th-century American movements (Stone-Campbell Restorationists, Latter-day Saints, Adventists, Bible Students) held that the historic Church had departed from New Testament Christianity. Some sought to restore primitive practice within Nicene faith; others (Latter-day Saints, Jehovah’s Witnesses) rejected the Nicene creed itself and are classed by the historic churches as outside orthodoxy.

sides.name: Restorationists (within Nicene faith)
sides.steelman: Christians are divided because they built creeds and traditions on top of Scripture. Let us lay them aside and restore the simple faith and practice of the New Testament church: immersion of believers, the Lord’s Supper each week, elders in each congregation and the name "Christian" alone.
counterArguments: The Bible needs a rule of faith

sides.name: Latter-day Saints
sides.steelman: After the apostles died, priesthood authority was lost. God the Father and his Son appeared to Joseph Smith and restored the Church with prophets, apostles, priesthood and further scripture. The Book of Mormon is another testament of Jesus Christ.
counterArguments: Departure from biblical monotheism and the Nicene Creed

sides.name: Jehovah’s Witnesses
sides.steelman: Soon after the apostles, Greek philosophy corrupted the Church with the Trinity, the immortal soul and hellfire. By careful Bible study we have restored the worship of Jehovah, the only true God, through his Son Jesus Christ, and proclaim his kingdom that began ruling in 1914.

sides.name: Historic Nicene churches
sides.steelman: Christ promised that the gates of hell would not prevail against his Church and that the Spirit would lead it into all truth. The creeds of Nicaea and Constantinople faithfully express the apostolic faith. Reform within the Church is always needed, but a total apostasy would make Christ’s promise void.

timeline.text: Cane Ridge revival, out of which Barton Stone’s movement grows.
Thomas Campbell’s Declaration and Address.
Book of Mormon published; Latter-day Saint church organised.
Stone and Campbell movements unite.
Joseph Smith killed at Carthage, Illinois; Millerite Great Disappointment.
Russell begins Zion’s Watch Tower.
LDS Manifesto ends official plural marriage.
Bible Students adopt the name Jehovah’s Witnesses.
LDS lifts priesthood restriction on Black men.
Catholic Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith rules LDS baptism invalid.

resolution.text: Stone-Campbell churches are generally accepted as Nicene Protestants. Latter-day Saints and Jehovah’s Witnesses remain outside the communion of Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches, which regard their doctrines of God as incompatible with the Nicene Creed; both movements regard themselves as the restored true Church.

consequences: Gave rise to several of the most successful American-born religious movements.
Sharpened debates about authority, the canon and the meaning of "Christian".
Shaped religious-liberty law through legal battles (especially Jehovah’s Witnesses).

controversies.question: Should divided churches seek visible unity?
controversies.title: Ecumenism and its critics
controversies.summary: The 20th-century ecumenical movement sought to overcome Christian divisions through councils, dialogues and church unions. Evangelicals, fundamentalists, some Orthodox and traditionalist Catholics questioned its methods and goals, while new forms of cooperation emerged.

sides.name: Ecumenists
sides.steelman: Christ prayed that his disciples might be one so that the world may believe. Our divisions are a scandal; we must pray, study and work together until we can share one table. Dialogue has already healed disputes that once seemed unbridgeable.
counterArguments: Unity at the expense of truth

sides.name: Evangelical cooperation without structural union
sides.steelman: True unity is spiritual and grounded in the gospel. We gladly cooperate with all who confess the biblical gospel in evangelism and service, but institutional union with churches that compromise Scripture would sacrifice truth.
counterArguments: Invisible unity is not what Jesus prayed for

sides.name: Separatists
sides.steelman: Scripture commands separation from those who deny the faith. The ecumenical movement embraces modernism and Rome; faithful churches must stand apart and contend for the truth.

timeline.text: World Missionary Conference, Edinburgh.
Stockholm Life and Work conference.
Lausanne Faith and Order conference.
Church of South India unites Anglicans, Methodists and Reformed.
World Council of Churches founded; fundamentalist International Council of Christian Churches formed in response.
Second Vatican Council opens.
Paul VI and Athenagoras lift the 1054 anathemas.
Lausanne Congress on World Evangelization.
Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry (Lima text).
Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification.
Pope Francis joins Lutherans in Lund to commemorate the Reformation; meets Patriarch Kirill in Havana.

resolution.text: Ongoing. Relations among churches have been transformed from hostility to cooperation, but full visible unity remains elusive, and new divisions over ethics and authority have appeared.

consequences: Created the WCC, regional councils and united churches.
Changed Catholic–Protestant and Catholic–Orthodox relations.
Stimulated parallel evangelical networks (Lausanne, World Evangelical Alliance).

people.name: Adolf von Harnack
people.summary: Baltic German church historian whose History of Dogma (1886–90) argued that dogma was the work of the Greek spirit on the soil of the gospel, and whose lectures What Is Christianity? (1900) distilled liberal Protestantism: the fatherhood of God, the infinite value of the human soul and the commandment of love. His former student Karl Barth broke with him after Harnack signed the 1914 manifesto supporting the German war effort.
keyIdeas: The kernel and husk of the gospel
Fatherhood of God and brotherhood of man

people.name: J. Gresham Machen
people.summary: Princeton New Testament scholar (The Origin of Paul’s Religion, 1921; The Virgin Birth of Christ, 1930) whose Christianity and Liberalism (1923) argued that liberalism was not a version of Christianity but a different religion. After Princeton Seminary was reorganised (1929) he founded Westminster Theological Seminary and, after his suspension from the ministry, the Orthodox Presbyterian Church (1936).
keyIdeas: Historic Christianity as a redemptive religion grounded in historical facts

people.name: Harry Emerson Fosdick
people.summary: The most famous liberal Protestant preacher in America. His sermon "Shall the Fundamentalists Win?" (21 May 1922), preached at First Presbyterian Church in New York, pleaded for tolerance of liberal views on the virgin birth, inerrancy and the second coming and ignited the Fundamentalist–Modernist controversy in the Presbyterian Church. He later served as pastor of Riverside Church (1930–46), and wrote the hymn "God of Grace and God of Glory".

people.name: Thomas Campbell
people.summary: Ulster Seceder Presbyterian minister who emigrated to western Pennsylvania (1807), was censured for offering communion to other Presbyterians, and founded the Christian Association of Washington, whose Declaration and Address (1809) called for Christian unity on the basis of the Bible alone. With his son Alexander he became a founder of the Stone-Campbell Restoration Movement.
keyIdeas: Unity through restoring New Testament Christianity
Rejection of creeds as tests of fellowship

people.name: Alexander Campbell
people.summary: Son of Thomas Campbell and the leading figure of the "Disciples" or "Reformers". After a period among Baptists he led an independent movement stressing believers’ immersion for the remission of sins, weekly communion and the New Testament as church constitution; in 1832 his followers united with Barton W. Stone’s "Christians". He edited The Christian Baptist and Millennial Harbinger and founded Bethany College (1840).
keyIdeas: Baptism for the remission of sins

people.name: Pope Pius X
people.summary: Giuseppe Sarto, pope from 1903 to 1914, who condemned Catholic Modernism in the decree Lamentabili and the encyclical Pascendi Dominici Gregis (1907), imposed the Anti-Modernist Oath on clergy (1910), encouraged frequent communion and the admission of children to communion, and began the codification of canon law. He was canonised in 1954.

people.name: John R. Mott
roles: YMCA and Student Volunteer Movement leader
people.summary: American Methodist layman who led the Student Volunteer Movement and the World Student Christian Federation, popularised the watchword "the evangelization of the world in this generation", chaired the World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh (1910) and helped found the International Missionary Council and the World Council of Churches.

people.name: Andrew F. Walls
people.summary: Scottish historian who taught in Sierra Leone and Nigeria and founded the Centre for the Study of Christianity in the Non-Western World (Aberdeen, later Edinburgh). His essays argued that Christianity is infinitely translatable, that its history is serial (its centre repeatedly moving), and that the 20th-century shift of its centre to Africa, Asia and Latin America is the most important development in recent church history.

people.name: Rachel Held Evans
people.summary: American writer raised in evangelical Tennessee whose books and blog (Faith Unraveled, 2010; A Year of Biblical Womanhood, 2012; Searching for Sunday, 2015; Inspired, 2018) gave voice to a generation questioning evangelical certainties about Scripture, gender, science and politics; she joined the Episcopal Church and became an emblematic figure in "deconstruction" and progressive Christianity before her early death.

works.title: The Christian Faith (Der christliche Glaube)
works.summary: Schleiermacher’s dogmatics, grounding doctrine in the Christian religious self-consciousness, the feeling of absolute dependence as shaped by Christ (1821–22; 2nd ed. 1830–31).
works.significance: The founding systematic theology of liberal Protestantism.

works.title: Declaration and Address of the Christian Association of Washington
works.summary: Thomas Campbell’s manifesto calling Christians to unite on the basis of the Bible alone, without creeds as terms of communion.
works.significance: Charter document of the Stone-Campbell Restoration Movement.

works.title: The Book of Mormon
works.summary: Published by Joseph Smith in Palmyra, New York, as a translation of ancient American records; regarded by Latter-day Saints as scripture alongside the Bible.
works.significance: Foundational scripture of the Latter-day Saint movement; not accepted as scripture by any Nicene church.

works.title: The Wentworth Letter (including the Articles of Faith)
works.summary: Joseph Smith’s account of the church’s origins for a Chicago editor, published in Times and Seasons (1 March 1842), ending with thirteen "Articles of Faith".
works.significance: The Articles of Faith became a canonised summary of Latter-day Saint belief (Pearl of Great Price).

works.title: The Divine Plan of the Ages (Millennial Dawn / Studies in the Scriptures, vol. 1)
works.summary: First volume of Charles Taze Russell’s series setting out the Bible Students’ chronology and theology.
works.significance: Foundational for the Bible Student movement and Jehovah’s Witnesses.

works.title: What Is Christianity? (Das Wesen des Christentums)
works.summary: Sixteen public lectures given in Berlin in the winter of 1899–1900.
works.significance: Classic popular statement of liberal Protestantism; English translation by T. B. Saunders (1901).

works.title: Pascendi Dominici Gregis
works.summary: Encyclical of Pius X on the doctrines of the Modernists.
works.significance: Condemned Catholic Modernism as "the synthesis of all heresies"; followed by the Anti-Modernist Oath (1910–1967).

works.title: The Evangelization of the World in This Generation
works.summary: John R. Mott’s exposition of the Student Volunteer Movement’s watchword.
works.significance: Expressed the confidence of the missionary movement on the eve of Edinburgh 1910.

works.title: The Fundamentals: A Testimony to the Truth
works.author: A. C. Dixon, Louis Meyer and R. A. Torrey (eds.)
works.summary: Ninety essays in twelve volumes (1910–15), funded by oilmen Lyman and Milton Stewart and edited by A. C. Dixon, Louis Meyer and R. A. Torrey, defending inerrancy, the virgin birth, the atonement, the resurrection and miracles, and criticising higher criticism, evolutionism, Romanism and new religions.
works.significance: About three million copies were distributed free to pastors, missionaries and students; gave "fundamentalism" its name.

works.title: Christianity and Liberalism
works.summary: Machen’s argument that liberalism and historic Christianity are two different religions, compared doctrine by doctrine.
works.significance: The most intellectually serious fundamentalist-era critique of liberalism; admired even by some secular critics such as Walter Lippmann.

works.title: Shall the Fundamentalists Win?
works.summary: Sermon preached at First Presbyterian Church, New York, 21 May 1922, and widely circulated in print.
works.significance: Triggered the Presbyterian phase of the Fundamentalist–Modernist controversy.

works.title: The Epistle to the Romans (Der Römerbrief)
works.summary: Karl Barth’s commentary on Romans (1919; radically rewritten 1922), stressing God’s otherness and judgement on all religion.
works.significance: Inaugurated "dialectical theology" or neo-orthodoxy; described as a bomb dropped on the theologians’ playground (Karl Adam).

works.title: Unitatis Redintegratio (Decree on Ecumenism)
works.summary: Vatican II’s decree on ecumenism, promulgated by Paul VI on 21 November 1964.
works.significance: Committed the Catholic Church to the ecumenical movement and recognised other Christians as brothers and sisters in the Lord.

works.title: The Lausanne Covenant
works.summary: Statement of the International Congress on World Evangelization (Lausanne, July 1974), drafted by a committee chaired by John Stott.
works.significance: Defining statement of global evangelicalism, affirming evangelism and social responsibility.

works.title: The Normal Christian Church Life
works.summary: Watchman Nee’s lectures on church order (originally in Chinese as Rethinking Our Work, 1938), teaching one church per locality led by local elders.
works.significance: Shaped the Local Church movement and Chinese indigenous and house-church ecclesiology.

works.title: The Missionary Movement in Christian History
works.summary: Collected essays by Andrew Walls on the transmission of the Christian faith across cultures.
works.significance: Influential framing of the southward shift of world Christianity.

works.title: Love Wins
works.summary: Rob Bell’s book questioning traditional teaching on hell and suggesting hope for universal reconciliation.
works.significance: A flashpoint in debates over progressive evangelicalism.

works.title: Searching for Sunday: Loving, Leaving, and Finding the Church
works.summary: Rachel Held Evans’ memoir of leaving evangelicalism and finding a home in the Episcopal Church, structured around the seven sacraments.

quotes.text: The self-identical essence of piety is this: the consciousness of being absolutely dependent, or, which is the same thing, of being in relation with God.
quotes.citation: Schleiermacher, The Christian Faith §4 (2nd ed. 1830; tr. H. R. Mackintosh and J. S. Stewart, 1928)

quotes.text: Where the Scriptures speak, we speak; and where the Scriptures are silent, we are silent.
quotes.citation: Thomas Campbell, address to the Christian Association of Washington, Pennsylvania (1809), as recorded in Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell (1868)

quotes.text: We believe the Bible to be the word of God as far as it is translated correctly; we also believe the Book of Mormon to be the word of God.
quotes.citation: Joseph Smith, Articles of Faith 8, in the Wentworth Letter, Times and Seasons (Nauvoo, 1 March 1842)

quotes.text: Russell taught that the Bible reveals a "divine plan of the ages" with a precise chronology, that Christ’s return would be an invisible presence, and that the "Gentile Times" would end in 1914; he rejected the Trinity, the immortality of the soul and eternal torment.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of Charles Taze Russell, The Divine Plan of the Ages (1886) and The Time Is at Hand (1889)

quotes.text: The Gospel, as Jesus proclaimed it, has to do with the Father only and not with the Son.
quotes.citation: Adolf von Harnack, What Is Christianity? (1900; tr. T. B. Saunders, 1901), Lecture 8
Pius X, Pascendi Dominici Gregis §39 (1907), describing Modernism as a system

quotes.text: The Evangelization of the World in This Generation
quotes.citation: Title and watchword of John R. Mott’s book (New York, 1900), adopted from the Student Volunteer Movement

quotes.text: Fosdick asked whether the churches would make room for Christians who, in the light of modern knowledge, did not hold to inerrancy, a biological virgin birth or a literal second coming, and pleaded for tolerance and liberty within the church rather than exclusion.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of Harry Emerson Fosdick, "Shall the Fundamentalists Win?" (sermon, 21 May 1922)

quotes.text: The great redemptive religion which has always been known as Christianity is battling against a totally diverse type of religious belief, which is only the more destructive of the Christian faith because it makes use of traditional Christian terminology.
quotes.citation: J. Gresham Machen, Christianity and Liberalism (1923), Introduction

quotes.text: Barth argued that God is "wholly other", that there is an infinite qualitative distinction (in Kierkegaard’s phrase) between God and humanity, and that God’s Word in Christ comes as judgement and grace upon all human religion, including the confident culture-Protestantism of his teachers.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of Karl Barth, The Epistle to the Romans (2nd ed. 1922), preface and on Romans 1

quotes.text: Nee taught that Scripture recognises one church in each locality, governed by local elders and not by foreign missions or denominations, so that Chinese churches should be self-governing, self-supporting and self-propagating under Christ.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of Watchman Nee, The Normal Christian Church Life (1938)

quotes.text: The Council declared that restoring unity among all Christians is one of its principal concerns, since division openly contradicts the will of Christ, scandalises the world and damages the preaching of the gospel; Christians of other communions, justified by faith in baptism, are recognised as brothers and sisters in the Lord.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of Unitatis Redintegratio 1 and 3 (21 November 1964)

quotes.text: The Lausanne Covenant affirmed that evangelism and socio-political involvement are both part of Christian duty, expressing penitence that evangelicals had sometimes regarded them as mutually exclusive, while insisting that reconciliation with people is not reconciliation with God.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of the Lausanne Covenant (1974), paragraph 5, "Christian Social Responsibility"

quotes.text: Walls argued that Christianity is infinitely translatable and has repeatedly moved its centre of gravity, from Jerusalem to the Hellenistic world, to northern Europe, and now to Africa, Asia and Latin America, so that the typical Christian today is no longer Western.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of Andrew F. Walls, The Missionary Movement in Christian History (1996), chs. 1 and 3

quotes.text: Bell questioned whether a loving God would consign billions to eternal torment, suggesting that God’s love may ultimately reconcile all things, and that this hope has been held within the Christian tradition before.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of Rob Bell, Love Wins (2011), chs. 3–4

quotes.text: Evans described leaving the evangelical church of her youth over questions of science, gender and the exclusion of LGBTQ people, and then finding faith renewed through the sacraments and liturgy of a mainline church, not as a return to certainty but to a community of grace.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of Rachel Held Evans, Searching for Sunday (2015)
